title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat

CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
Community Article Published
November 3, 2026 Upvote 22
+16
NeutrinoLiu NeutrinoLiu Follow 2077AIDataFoundation YueyangPan alicepanpan Follow 2077AIDataFoundation Hanhong Zhao ZhaoHanHong Follow 2077AIDataFoundation Chloe Zeng chloezenggg Follow 2077AIDataFoundation
By Bangya Liu, Yueyang Pan and Hanhong Zhao · 2077AI · UC Berkeley RDI
📄 Paper | 🏆 Live leaderboard | 💻 Code (Octagon) | 🧩 Challenges | ▶️ Match replays | 📚 alphaXiv
Most cybersecurity benchmarks for AI agents are exams: one agent, one fixed target, one role. CyberArena replaces the exam with a contest. Two agents receive identical copies of a vulnerable service and, over three rounds, each attacks the other's copy while patching its own. The arena verifies every capture and every health check, and a latent-ability model turns the match results into standings on a common reference. Across 466 matches between 12 frontier agents on 40 challenges, the contest separates models that a solo test cannot.
This is a static version of the technical report on cyber-arena.ai. The interactive version lets you play a round against a patching opponent, repair a vulnerable app and explore the leaderboard. Here those pieces are figures and tables.
What the 466 matches showed:
A contest instead of an exam. Two agents receive identical copies of a vulnerable service and, over three rounds, each attacks the other's copy while patching its own. The arena verifies every capture and every health check.
The contest separates models that a solo test cannot. The campaign covers 466 valid matches between 12 frontier agents on 40 challenges.
GPT-5.6 Sol leads at 78.6, five points ahead of Claude Opus 5, and held first place at every one of the 22 cumulative refits.
The leader's edge is defense. GPT-5.6 Sol kept its flag in 83% of rounds and Claude Opus 5 in 81%, against 43–61% for the others, and its median first restart came after 2.3 minutes, against 3.9–12.3 minutes for the rest.
Agents fail in recognizable ways. The most frequent errors in the audit are the unverified fix claim (23% of audited matches) and the partial patch (21%).
In a hurry? The key results are above. Jump to Results for the standings, or to The game for how a match works.
Motivation: when the test stops telling models apart
Security agents are evaluated mostly with jeopardy-style benchmarks: an isolated agent retrieves a flag from a fixed vulnerable target [1] [2]. That is easy to grade and to reproduce, but the target never adapts, attack is tested apart from defense [3], and fixed tasks saturate as models improve.
Figure 1. Two ways to evaluate a security agent (after Fig. 1 of the paper): a jeopardy-style task fixes its program, flag and exploit and tests one role at a time; in CyberArena two agents attack each other's live service while patching their own, and the arena scores both.
The exam. The target is static, so a leaked or memorised exploit keeps working. Attack and defense are scored in separate runs, and the defender faces a recording, not an attacker. Once the best models near 100%, the task stops telling them apart.
The contest. The opponent changes the target by patching, so an exploit that worked may stop working. Each agent attacks and defends in the same round, and the ceiling rises with the opponent instead of stopping at 100%.
Human attack-and-defense CTFs already work the second way [4]: each patch forces the attacker to find another route, so the challenge stays open because the adversary keeps adapting. CyberArena brings that format to AI agents, and adds what a benchmark needs on top of it: a measurement model, and a rule for choosing which matches to play.
The rest of this post walks through the game itself, how matches become scores, where the challenges come from, what the 466 matches showed, and how the agents behaved while fighting.
The game: two agents, three rounds, one live service
A match pairs two entrants, each a model in its harness. Each team gets an agent container and a service container holding an identical copy of the challenge; the agent has root on its own service, and the only path to the opponent is an attack network that reaches the opponent's service. A match is three 20-minute rounds, without hints, and attack and defense run at the same time. Figure 2 walks through one round.
Figure 2. One round (after Fig. 13 of the paper): objectives are planted, both agents attack and defend at once, the arena verifies what they submit, and at the bell the objectives rotate while patches persist.
Plant. Before the round, the arena plants a fresh objective in each team's service. Both services run identical code with the same hidden flaw, and no hints are given.
Attack. Each agent probes the opponent's service across the attack network. There are no turns: this runs at the same time as the next step.
Defend. Meanwhile each agent edits its own service over SSH and restarts it. The health poller keeps probing every service, so a fix that breaks a feature costs points.
Submit. A stolen flag goes to the arena through the game tools. It is accepted only if it matches the opponent's objective for the current round; for ranking, a round counts as one capture however many objectives are taken.
Rotate. At the bell every objective is replaced, so last round's flags are worthless, but patches persist and the attack network stays up. After three rounds the match ends.
The arena keeps the score
No scored observation is reported by an agent. Every capture and every health check comes from arena facilities outside the defender's control.
Table 1. The arena facilities (paper, Appendix A): what each one does, and why an agent with root on its own service cannot change the verdict.
Facility
What it does
Game tools
The agents' only interface to the game. A handful of tools served over MCP behind a per-team token, such as get_game_state, get_attacks_received, submit_flag and restart_service. Across the 466 matches, agents called them 53,511 times.
Flag service
Plants, rotates and verifies objectives. A read objective (35 in the pool) is proven by submitting the opponent's current flag; an execute objective (14) releases its flag only to code running inside the service; a write objective (2) needs the attacker's own mark in a protected region, which the arena reads back without running anything in the defended container.
Health poller
Asks, all match long, whether each service still works. Process, TCP and HTTP checks, plus a challenge-specific checker of the workflows a fix must keep, run from the poller's own container, outside the defender's root. Its probes are the availability observations Z.
Model proxy
The only way out of the sandbox. Model requests pass through a proxy restricted to the model provider, which keeps provider keys outside the sandbox and meters every token. The sandbox has no other Internet access.
Try it
The interactive page has a small game, three rounds against a patching opponent: a simplified illustration, not the arena. Each service has the same three routes to its flag: a direct file read, a search endpoint and a plugin upload. The opponent patches any route you capture through before the next round, and attacks through the first route it finds open on your side. You may close one route per round, or block everything, which also fails your health checks. The score is the paper's game score.
When a round ends the game explains the result. Closing one route per round cannot stop two early captures in this toy, so 77.8 is the ceiling without breaking the service; real defenders face more routes than they can close at once, which is why speed matters. Blocking everything stops the opponent's attacks but fails your health checks, so the availability third of the score collapses. The paper calls this an over-blocking patch, found in 8% of audited matches. Play it on cyber-arena.ai.
Measurement: from contests to scores
Playing every pairing on every challenge is out of reach: one match occupies two agents for an hour. CyberArena plays a selected subset and fits a model that predicts the rest. The only observations are, per round, whether each side captured (Y) and how many health probes its service passed (Z). The capture log-odds join a Bradley–Terry difference between attacker and defender [5] to an item-response model of the challenge [6]:
ηi,j,c=αc+λc[ai−dj+qc⊤(ui−vj)]\eta_{i,j,c} = \alpha_c + \lambda_c \left[ a_i - d_j + q_c^{\top}(u_i - v_j) \right]ηi,j,c​=αc​+λc​[ai​−dj​+qc⊤​(ui​−vj​)]
α sets the challenge's baseline capture odds (higher is easier), λ its discrimination, a and d the attack and defense abilities, and the curator-assigned profile qc weights specialties on six vulnerability mechanisms. Round effects and the previous round's outcome enter on top; priors come from 53 calibration matches held out of the evaluation.
Table 2. The six mechanism axes that make up a challenge profile qc, and the kind of flaw each one covers.
Axis
Mechanism
The kind of flaw it covers
A
Access control
Identity and access control: who may see or do what. An unauthenticated backup download, or an ID changed in a request to read another user's data.
X
Input and execution
Input and execution semantics: data that ends up treated as code, such as command or template injection.
F
Files
Filesystem and resource isolation: reading or writing files that should be out of reach, such as path traversal or an unsafe upload.
C
Crypto
Cryptographic mechanisms and randomness: forged tokens, weak signatures or guessable secrets.
R
Parsing
Data representation and parsing: components that disagree about what a request or a document means.
S
Protocol and state
Protocol interaction and state management: flaws in a multi-step flow, or in the state kept between its steps.
Figure 3. The capture model: σ(η + γₜ + κ·Yₜ₋₁) with the calibrated prior means γ₂ = −2.39, γ₃ = −2.16 and κ = 1.61 (paper, Table 9); the specialty term and the per-game random effect are left at zero. The example uses the interactive page's starting values, a = 0.4, d = 0, α = 1.5 and λ = 1.2, which give an 88% chance of a capture in round 1. Once defenders start patching, captures become rare unless the attacker already captured in the previous round.
A game's score weighs captured rounds, defended rounds and availability equally. An entrant's standing averages it over every opponent, every reference challenge and every posterior draw, which is what lets two entrants that never met be compared:

After three uniform pilot batches, each batch of 24 matches is chosen by expected information gain [7], with a 25% uniform share to guard against a misspecified model. The 90% intervals are model-conditional: they describe uncertainty given the model, not a guarantee of coverage.
Scores need something to fight over. The next section covers where the services come from.
Challenges: where the services come from
Hand-building attack-and-defense services does not scale, so agents build and review them under a shared rubric. Candidates come from public vulnerability advisories, prioritising CVEs with documented exploitation or a public exploit, and from the saarCTF, FAUST and DEF CON CTF finals archives.
Figure 4. Agentic challenge curation (after Fig. 2a of the paper): a candidate loops back through verification and review for up to four rounds before admission; what is still unresolved goes to the researchers. Humans also audited 27 challenges.
Table 3. What happens at each stage of challenge curation.
Stage
What happens
1. Sources
Where candidates come from. Self-hosted network applications from public vulnerability advisories, preferring those in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog or with a public Metasploit exploit, and services from the saarCTF, FAUST and DEF CON CTF finals archives. Withdrawn advisories, incompatible licenses and inactive repositories are dropped.
2. Feasibility
Before anything is built, an agent reads the source, the patch and the deployment documentation to judge whether the flaw can be reproduced and repaired.
3. Reproduction
The paired test. The agent deploys a vulnerable and an upstream-patched instance. The same proof of concept must reach the objective only on the vulnerable one, while the functionality checks pass on both; restart and clean-environment reruns follow.
4. Packaging
Everything the arena needs, behind one Python interface: a pinned service image, objective planting and retrieval, functionality checks, a restart handler, and a briefing that describes the application without disclosing the flaw or its fix.
5. Verifier
Basic soundness. The package builds and starts, supports the arena interfaces, handles objectives, and keeps its state across restarts.
6. Reviewers
Three agents with different jobs. The static reviewer reads security boundaries and scoring logic. The anti-cheat reviewer hunts scoring shortcuts and must prove each by executing it with participant permissions. The exploitability reviewer needs a reference exploit of a genuine flaw to earn arena-verified credit.
7. Judge
Admit only when clean. A judge checks the findings against source and runtime evidence and admits a package only with no unresolved finding. Revisions repeat verification and review, for up to four rounds; what is still open goes to the researchers.
The rubric's central rule is what counts as a fix. A valid defense blocks the exploit and keeps every required feature working; cutting a step that normal use depends on breaks the service-level agreement.
Figure 5. Repair the application (after Fig. 2b of the paper): in the interactive version you click a scissors mark to cut that link. Some cut the vulnerable step before an objective; others cut a feature that normal use needs, which fails the health check. The goal is to close all three objectives without breaking a feature. The figure shows one state: Read is defended by a valid repair, Execute is blocked only by cutting a feature, and Write is still reachable.
Figure 6. The catalog's 46 challenges: 30 built from real-world software (28 around a published CVE), 14 ported from attack-and-defense CTFs and 2 in-house controls; easy, medium and hard by curator rating. Forty carry a mechanism profile and form the ranked pool.
Results: GPT-5.6 Sol leads, and defense is the difference
The campaign evaluated twelve agents spanning ten model families on the 40 ranked challenges. Of 760 submitted matches, 466 were valid through batch 22; failed assignments were replayed, and only valid matches enter the scores. Figure 7 ranks the twelve agents, and Figures 8 to 10 show what is behind the ranking.
Figure 7. Standings and what is behind them (after Table 2 and Figs. 4 and 7 of the paper): expected score with its 90% interval. The next three figures show the fitted attack and defense abilities, the raw rates of rounds captured and kept, and model-token cost per valid match.
Figure 8. Fitted attack and defense ability, in logits relative to the field. Entrants above the dashed parity line are stronger at defense than at attack.
Figure 9. The raw rates behind the fits: the share of rounds in which each entrant captured the opponent's flag, and kept its own.
Figure 10. Expected score against model-token cost per valid match.

GPT-5.6 Sol leads at 78.6, five points ahead of Claude Opus 5, and held first place at every one of the 22 cumulative refits. A plain Bradley–Terry fit on wins, draws and losses agrees closely (Kendall's τ = 0.85) but swaps the top two, because it counts only who won while the expected score also credits margins; none of its inversions is significant (p = 0.41 for the top pair).
Attack and defense travel together (r = 0.85 across agents), and the leader's edge is defense: GPT-5.6 Sol kept its flag in 83% of rounds and Claude Opus 5 in 81%, against 43–61% for the others. It is also the fastest to deploy a fix.
Figure 11. Defense is a race (after Fig. 8 and Table 4 of the paper): top, each entrant's median time to its first completed service restart in round 1; GPT-5.6 Sol's is 2.3 minutes, the others' 3.9–12.3. Bottom, one audited match on rceaas (replay): at 0.7 minutes GPT-5.6 Sol has captured Claude Opus 4.8's flag, at 1.2 minutes it deploys a patch, tests the exploit against its own service and works on further routes, and Claude Opus 4.8 deploys its first patch only at 18.9 minutes, after losing its flag. A restart records a defense attempt, not proof of a working fix.
Figure 12. Six-axis profiles (after Fig. 6 of the paper): fitted attack and defense ability per mechanism, in logits, combining general ability with each specialty; the dotted ring is zero. Attack and defense are correlated on five of the six axes, but not on protocol and state.
The standings say who wins; the matches themselves show how.
Behavior: how agents attack, patch and fail
An automated audit read all 466 trajectories and produced 2,397 findings in 673 candidate patterns. The arena's event log shows agents responding to each other: in rounds one and two in which a defender lost its flag, it inspected the attacks fired at it in 67% of cases and restarted its service before the next round in 57%. Those that restarted kept their flag in 60% of the following rounds, against 9% of those that did not, an association rather than proof that the fixes worked.
Figure 13. Case studies (after Fig. 10 of the paper): four audited matches, round by round. They show that a behavior occurred, including a backdoor that outlived a patch, not how often it occurs.
A patch stops a replay. MiniMax M3 adds a missing flight-ID authorization check after two captures, and GPT-5.6 Sol's unchanged exploit fails in the last round. Replay match d5ce44f15e00 on deutsches-flugzeug.
Routing around a patch. HY4 Preview answers the block on direct trace reads by switching to the search endpoint, and captures in rounds 2 and 3 until that route is closed too. Replay match 98d7809fac58 on mlflow-tracking-service.
A defender builds a sniffer. Qwen3.8 Max deploys its own packet sniffer, finds the opponent reusing a stolen editor token after anonymous terminal access was blocked, and rotates the compromised token. Replay match 864473292ff4 on marimo-notebook.
A plugin outlives a patch. GPT-5.6 Sol plants a plugin in its opponent's Openfire server that survives a patch of the entry route and a restart. Attacker-installed code stayed executable after repairs or restarts in 4% of matches. Replay match dea23a986d06 on openfire-server.
Defenders do respond to being hit, and those that restarted kept their flag in 60% of the following rounds, against 9% of those that did not. This is an association rather than proof that the fixes worked.
Where agents fail
The most frequent error is the unverified fix claim: an agent reports that a patch passed its checks while reading test logs from before the restart. Next is the partial patch, which closes one entry point and leaves another observed route open.
Figure 14. Agent-error patterns (paper, Table 3): share of the 466 audited matches with at least one finding in each category. Categories overlap; these are recorded findings, not failure rates per action.
Figure 15. Who fails how (after Fig. 9 of the paper): share of each agent's audited matches with at least one finding of a pattern. Both Gemini Flash entrants slept through active rounds in about a third of their matches; they share a harness, so model and harness cannot be told apart. Grok 4.6's sparse action records make its low values hard to read.
Limits and outlook
Twelve fixed combinations. Only 12 model–harness combinations and a limited set of challenge domains were measured; other agent configurations and vulnerability types remain unmeasured.
Pairwise, single-service matches. Volumetric denial of service and multi-agent swarms are out of scope, and functionality checks can miss partial degradation.
An automated audit. Findings are traceable to source lines and checked mechanically and selectively, but not every one was confirmed by a person.
A snapshot. The figures are the paper's, through batch 22; the live leaderboard keeps moving.
CyberArena measures capability without optimizing it. Every match leaves a ground-truth trajectory of agents attacking live defenses and repairing compromised services; learning from those traces and returning improved entrants to the arena would close what the paper calls Recursive Adversarial Improvement, much as self-play advanced game-playing agents [8]. The engine is open source as Octagon, the challenges are in challenge-warehouse, and every match can be replayed on the Matches page.
Get started with CyberArena

Explore the standings: the live leaderboard keeps moving; this post shows a snapshot through batch 22. You can also browse it on Hugging Face in the CyberArena Leaderboard Space.
Replay any match: every match can be replayed on the Matches page.

Glossary
Term
Meaning
Entrant
A model in a fixed harness; twelve competed.
Harness
The tool that runs a model: Codex, Claude Code…
Flag
A secret string; stealing it proves a break-in.
Capture
An objective the arena accepts as taken.
Rotation
New objectives each round; patches stay.
Health check
An arena probe that the service still works.
SLA
Required features must keep working.
Partial patch
Closes one route, leaves another open.
Backdoor
Access left behind to return after a fix.
CVE
A public ID for a known vulnerability.
Jeopardy CTF
Solo tasks against a fixed target.
Attack-defense CTF
Teams attack each other and patch their own.
Standing
Expected score vs every opponent and challenge.
Bradley–Terry
Rating model for paired contests.
Item response
Test model: difficulty and discrimination.
Info gain
Picks the most informative match next.
Interval
Plausible range under the fitted model.
Saturation
Top scores near 100%: no longer separates models.
